notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, as the county reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
The county borrowed $3,189,000 during the year, which is not counted as revenue but helps explain spending above revenue.
Payments to other governments ($3,038,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts cash contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to county commissioner, council, executive, sheriff, prosecutor and other county office candidates, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023. Washington allows business and union contributions to local candidates. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and caucus committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Thurston County Sheriff's Office operates one DJI Matrice 210 drone as of 2018, according to data compiled by the Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College.

notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, as the city reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. Residents also pay Thurston County.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
The city borrowed $4,207,000 during the year, which is not counted as revenue but helps explain spending above revenue.
Payments to other governments ($197,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts cash contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to candidates for mayor and council, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023. Washington allows business and union contributions to local candidates. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and caucus committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 8 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Lacey's borders in OpenStreetMap (7 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 7 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Lacey's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.

notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, as the city reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. Residents also pay Thurston County.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
The city borrowed $1,819,000 during the year, which is not counted as revenue but helps explain spending above revenue.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts cash contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to candidates for mayor and council, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023. Washington allows business and union contributions to local candidates. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and caucus committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 9 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Olympia's borders in OpenStreetMap (7 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 7 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Olympia's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.

Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
Payments to other governments ($29,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts cash contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to candidates for mayor and council, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023. Washington allows business and union contributions to local candidates. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and caucus committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 6 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Yelm's borders in OpenStreetMap (6 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.
